\title{Diagnosing and Repairing Minimal-Data Activation Probes for LLM Safety}

\author{\uppercase{Glen Messenger}\authorrefmark{1}}
\address[1]{Google Cloud, Google LLC, Sunnyvale, CA 94089 USA (e-mail: gmessenger@google.com)}
\tfootnote{The author is supported by Google LLC. ORCID: 0009-0009-1802-4725.}

\markboth%
{Messenger: Diagnosing and Repairing Minimal-Data Activation Probes for LLM Safety}%
{Messenger: Diagnosing and Repairing Minimal-Data Activation Probes for LLM Safety}

\corresp{Corresponding author: Glen Messenger (e-mail: gmessenger@google.com).}

\begin{abstract}
Linear probes on language-model activations are an appealing safety mechanism: they add microseconds and
kilobytes to inference already being performed, and probe-based monitoring has recently entered production use at
frontier labs. A practical question for settings without frontier-scale training data is how far this approach
stretches in the minimal-data regime, where probes are trained on tens of contrastive examples. We evaluate this
regime across seven open models from three architecture families, on harmful-content detection, prompt-injection
detection, and policy compliance, and find that reported outcomes are dominated by two factors that have received
little scrutiny: extraction convention and evaluation design. Probes that appear to fail --- flagging 30--94\% of
topic-matched benign prompts, or scoring near chance on real prompt-injection benchmarks --- are substantially
repaired by changing where the activation is read, not how the probe is trained: reading prompts through the model's
chat template raises length-stratified harmful-content AUC by $+0.30$ to $+0.54$ on all seven models (to
$0.92$--$0.98$, exceeding tuned lexical baselines by $+0.21$ to $+0.27$), and reading the mean over the tool-response
span instead of the final token raises injection detection from $0.58$--$0.86$ to $0.94$--$0.97$ AUC on injections
never seen in training. Conversely, we retire a proposed training method --- paired contrastive learning --- by
showing its estimator is algebraically identical to standard contrastive training and its data construction
contributes nothing measurable; we show that probes cannot linearly separate encoded-harmful from encoded-benign
prompts at any layer, even for encodings the model demonstrably decodes, and that training on encoded examples
manufactures perfect apparent detection while flagging all encoded benign inputs; and we show that for short authored
text, directive force is lexically constituted, so short-text authored evaluations cannot certify semantic claims for
any compliance classifier. Along the way we document exploitable label artifacts in the InjecAgent benchmark; prompt
length as a pervasive confound, separating one standard benchmark's harmful and benign classes at AUC $0.95$ and
inflating unstratified scores elsewhere ($0.90$ falling to $0.58$ under stratification); a tensor-identity hazard in
vLLM activation hooks; the necessity of separating probe detections from the model's own refusals; and the invalidity
of leave-one-out cross-validation on minimal-pair data. We distill these into a pre-registered evaluation protocol ---
including three cases where pre-registered designs proved unable to answer their own questions --- and release all
datasets, probes, and provenance-stamped results. Minimal-data activation probes can work; whether they do is decided
by conventions most papers never report.
\end{abstract}

% Author biography, no photograph (not required for this submission).
\begin{IEEEbiographynophoto}{Glen Messenger}
is a product management lead at Google Cloud, working on AI infrastructure security and AI safety. His research
focuses on representation engineering for LLM safety and inference security, with contributions spanning
activation-based model verification, runtime safety enforcement, inference scheduling, and KV-cache compression; his
work on detecting safety-training modification via activation analysis appears in IEEE Access. His open-source work
includes the Activation Model Scanner (AMS) and k8s-aibom, a Kubernetes-native AI bill-of-materials framework. Prior
to Google, he co-founded a B2B network security startup, and held senior security architecture roles in Finance and
Government. He holds a CCIE certification and is a named inventor on patents spanning firewall management and AI
inference security.
\end{IEEEbiographynophoto}
